# Regional Elections Monitor: Runoff Election in Brazil


October 26, 2026


**Economic Studies Department**


Sergio Olarte | Gustavo Acero


This analysis, prepared by our Economic Research Department, examines the outcome of Brazil’s presidential runoff and its implications for the country’s political landscape. It also highlights the challenges ahead for governability, fiscal sustainability, and investor confidence.


Key Takeaways of the Week


- Lula secured a fourth term in office—his second consecutive term—after coming from behind in the runoff. Following Flávio Bolsonaro’s unexpected lead in the first round, Lula significantly expanded his vote share and won with 51.79% of the vote, a margin of approximately 4.4 million votes. Voter turnout reached 80.78%, while abstention fell to its lowest level in a presidential runoff since 2006.
- The result confirmed the country’s geographic polarization and left regional power fragmented. Lula consolidated his support in the Northeast and managed to flip Minas Gerais, while Bolsonaro maintained his dominance in the South and Center-West. At the same time, the PL secured more governorships than the PT, meaning that Lula’s presidential victory did not translate into comparable territorial dominance.
- Governability will depend on agreements with centrist and right-wing parties. The limited congressional presence of Lula’s allies and the strengthening of the Liberal Party will require the administration to build consensus to advance its agenda. The composition of Congress will serve as an institutional check, limiting the scope for disruptive policy changes.
- With electoral uncertainty now resolved, attention is shifting to fiscal sustainability. The composition of the cabinet and the credibility of the fiscal adjustment plan will be key determinants of investor confidence, against a backdrop of elevated debt and fiscal deficits.
